BBC

Watchdog calls for pause on AI data centres in Wales

Data centres providing online services already exist in towns including Slough

A Welsh watchdog has called for a pause on the approval of new AI data centres until safeguards are in place.

Future Generations Commissioner Derek Walker said decisions about large-scale projects should not be made without their long-term impact being taken into account.

It follows moves by the Welsh government to take responsibility for the planning process for a scheme in Cardiff because of the \"substantial controversy\" the plans had generated.

The Welsh government said it believed in a \"balanced approach\" to data centres.

Ministers are currently considering their own national policy for data centres in Wales - Welsh government minister Adam Price said he was creating a \"Made in Wales\" version of the UK government's data centre covenant.

The future generations commissioner's role is to encourage public bodies to consider the long-term consequences of decisions, and to monitor that public bodies are complying with the Wellbeing of Future Generations Act.

Walker wants assurances that the act was being applied to decisions relating to AI infrastructure, and said environmental, social, cultural and economic effects be examined before projects are given the go-ahead.

He said there should be a halt on new developments before national guidance and safeguards are in place.

Walker said: \"Artificial intelligence will play an important role in Wales' future, and we should welcome opportunities for responsible innovation and investment - but we cannot afford to make decisions about major new data centres without fully understanding the long-term consequences and involving communities directly.\"

\"These developments will place significant demands on our energy and water resources, with implications for our environment, the communities living nearby and for our climate commitments.\"

Data centres have been controversial worldwide, in large part because of the power and cooling requirements of the chips required by recent AI technologies.

In Wales, campaigners have focused on plans for a data centre at a park and ride for a hospital in Cardiff.

The night before the local council's planning committee was due to discuss an application for permission for the scheme, the Welsh government called the project in.

Officials said \"substantial controversy\" meant it should be determined by the Welsh government.

Developers were also looking at building a centre between Caernarfon and Y Felinheli in Gwynedd.

The Welsh government said it was developing a planning policy for data centres and \"will publish an update before the end of the year, setting out the key principles to guide their development\".

In an interview with BBC Wales earlier this week, Enterprise Minister Adam Price said the government wanted to establish a policy that would avoid some of the problems seen elsewhere.

\"The Wales of the future and the Wales of now needs digital infrastructure, including data centres,\" he said.

However, he said ministers wanted developments to be located in areas where energy and grid capacity were available and to avoid public opposition driven by concerns about water use and power consumption.

\"We're creating a 'Made in Wales' version of the UK government's data centre covenant,\" Price added, arguing that a clearer framework would support investors and local communities.

The UK government's Data Centre Covenant said the UK will need 6GW of AI data centre capacity by 2030 to protect the country's national interest.

It says the covenant sets expectations for developers to minimise water use, pay their \"fair share\" of energy costs and \"deliver benefits for local communities\".

A Welsh government spokesperson said: \"We believe in a sustainable and balanced approach to developing data centres. We recognise that data centres are energy intensive.

\"As demand for digital infrastructure grows, it is important that new developments make use of technologies and approaches that minimise energy and resource consumption.

\"Any proposed data centre development remains subject to the existing planning system and environmental regulation, with robust checks and balances in place to ensure that environmental and community impacts are properly considered before consent is granted.

\"Wales is increasingly being recognised as a strategic location for the infrastructure needed to support the digital economy.

\"Investment in data centres has the potential to create new economic opportunities and support skilled employment. But the Welsh government believes that the benefits of any investment must be felt by businesses, communities and in the wider Welsh economy.\"
